title: Network Topology Segmentation
business: Telecommunications infrastructure providers managing large-scale fiber optic networks.
problem: The provider struggles to identify if two disparate network segments are physically connected through a series of intermediate switches, leading to redundant maintenance dispatches and inefficient routing.
solution: Disjoint-Set Union (DSU) maintains nonoverlapping sets of connected switches. By performing a Union operation when a new link is established and a Find operation to check connectivity, the provider can instantly determine if two segments belong to the same network partition.
steps: Initialize each network switch as a unique set where it is its own parent.
Execute a Find operation with path compression to locate the representative root of a switch's network segment.
Perform a Union operation to merge two sets when a physical cable connects two previously separate segments.
Verify connectivity by comparing the root representatives of two switches using the Find operation.
outcome: Reduced operational overhead by preventing redundant field technician dispatches for already connected network segments.
limitation: The primary limitation is the lack of support for edge removal; once two sets are merged, they cannot be split without rebuilding the structure, which can be checked by monitoring if the network topology requires frequent dynamic disconnections.

options: It cannot handle more than 100 switches.
It lacks support for removing existing connections.
It requires a central server for every operation.
It is slower than a simple linked list.
